item.description: Full title: How Tamnoon built AI-powered cloud security remediation with Amazon Bedrock
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

How Tamnoon built AI-powered cloud security remediation with Amazon Bedrock

Critical cloud exposures pile up faster than security teams can close them. Cloud-native application protection platforms (CNAPP), cloud providers, and posture scanners generate more findings than any team can triage, and risk accumulates in the gap between detected and fixed. Most findings sit untouched, not because they’re hard to fix. Someone must investigate context, identify the owner, confirm the fix won’t break production, and then do it at a volume that outpaces headcount.

In this post, we share how Tamnoon built Tami, an agentic cloud remediation orchestrator on Amazon Bedrock, to close that gap. Tami autonomously investigates findings ingested from CNAPP and cloud-native sources and assesses whether remediation is safe. It then generates and orchestrates the fix with guardrails and governance wherever a change touches a customer’s cloud. The approach drove an over 90 percent reduction in critical cloud exposure in 90 days with zero production issues.

About Tamnoon

Tamnoon is an AI-powered cloud security remediation platform that works alongside CNAPPs. Its AI assistant, Tami, helps human cloud security experts investigate, prioritize, and safely remediate misconfigurations and issues across customer environments in AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and other cloud providers.

Tamnoon integrates with the CNAPPs and cloud-native tools teams already use and turns their findings into validated, production-safe fixes. Most of the work including investigation, prioritization, and remediation planning happens before anything touches a live environment, which is what makes automated remediation trustworthy at scale.

Cloud security remediation challenges

A security engineer can spend hours investigating a single finding. Often, it traces back to the same root cause as dozens of other alerts.

  • Alert volume overwhelms headcount: CNAPPs and scanners generate thousands of findings. Teams can’t triage them all, so critical exposures sit unresolved while risk compounds for months.
  • Investigation is manual and repetitive: Each finding requires context gathering on who owns the resource, what depends on it, whether the fix is safe. This eats hours of senior engineer time, repeated across every item in the backlog.
  • Fear of production impact blocks automation: Teams hesitate to automate remediation because they can’t risk taking down production. Without confidence that a fix is safe, nothing moves.
  • Reactive prioritization: Without a way to cluster related findings or score remediation confidence, teams work through alerts linearly rather than addressing root causes that resolve many issues at once.

Tamnoon’s solution addresses the full pipeline from finding ingestion to validated fix. The platform treats these challenges as interconnected rather than isolated problems.

Solution overview

Tamnoon takes you from initial finding to executing the fix. The platform ingests findings from CNAPP, Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) providers, and other security tools and normalizes them into a unified schema. It then enriches them with asset and exposure context and prioritizes them. From there, the agentic layer takes over using a set of specialized AI agents, each running in an event-driven, serverless architecture on AWS, so every stage scales independently and fails safely.

Agentic architecture on Amazon Bedrock

The platform delegates work to four specialized agents, each responsible for a distinct phase of the remediation pipeline:

  • An investigation agent draws on training from millions of real customer cloud environments to determine context, filters that context through a large language model (LLM)-as-a-judge validation layer. It reasons through the remediation goal, operational scope, and cloud-provider-specific verification, producing read-only investigation steps and a complete investigation plan.
  • A safety-scoring agent builds an evidence chain per asset, combining automated verification results with analyst findings. It classifies each finding’s remediation as SAFE, RISKY, or AWAITING DATA with a deliberately conservative bias. When in doubt, it downgrades.
  • A remediation agent activates only for findings that the safety agent has deemed safe. It reasons through ordering, dependencies, and conditions, then produces a remediation plan in which every step follows a backup, remediate, and verify structure and includes rollback guidance.
  • A code-generation agent turns plan steps into executable remediation, but only after an input guardrail screens for relevance and prompt injection. Every artifact passes an automated generate-and-review loop in which a separate reviewer agent must approve the output.

Why Amazon Bedrock

When the Tamnoon team set out to build Tami, the choice of foundation model (FM) platform was going to shape everything that followed. Tamnoon’s remediation agents don’t all do the same kind of work. Some perform deep investigative reasoning to understand the root cause of a security finding. Others handle high-volume validation, checking proposed fixes quickly and cheaply. Still others review generated code, balancing quality against cost on every task. Matching each of these jobs to the right model, without stitching together a different integration for each one, was a core requirement.

That requirement is what made Amazon Bedrock the natural fit. Through a single API, each agent can call the foundation model best suited to its task. The most capable models handle the hardest reasoning. More efficient models take on the repetitive, high-throughput work. Review-focused models optimize the trade-off between output quality and cost. Because it’s one integration rather than many, models can be swapped or upgraded as the landscape evolves, without re-plumbing the architecture each time.

Operational overhead at scale was another factor in the decision. As request volume grew, Tamnoon wanted to avoid building and maintaining its own logic to distribute traffic across regional capacity. Amazon Bedrock Cross-Region inference handles this automatically. It automatically routes inference requests to the optimal AWS Region within a defined geographic boundary, maintaining throughput without requiring any custom routing code to operate.

Security was the final consideration, and for a cloud security company it was non-negotiable. With Bedrock, inference runs inside Tamnoon’s own AWS environment under AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)-scoped permissions. Sensitive customer data never leaves the trust boundary. That gave the team confidence that the platform underpinning Tami met the same standard Tamnoon holds its own service to.

How Tamnoon integrates with CNAPPs and cloud security tools

Tamnoon sits downstream of the detection tools security teams already run. CNAPPs like Wiz, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Cortex, Upwind, SentinelOne, Orca, and Cyera along with cloud-native services like AWS Security Hub and Amazon GuardDuty are the source of truth for what’s wrong in the environment. Tamnoon connects through API-based integrations and normalizes findings into a common format, so a misconfiguration looks the same whether it came from Wiz or GuardDuty. The detection tools remain the foundation. Tamnoon delivers the end-to-end remediation that follows.

For every finding it works, Tami assigns a Remediation Confidence Indicator (RCI) of SAFE, RISKY, or AWAITING DATA. That rating tells teams what can be automated and what needs human review first.

Figure 1: Tamnoon in action

Tamnoon AWS architecture

Tamnoon runs entirely within its own AWS accounts, isolated per environment. Users access the platform through a single secure entry point built on Amazon API Gateway, with encryption managed by AWS Certificate Manager and sign-in handled by Amazon Cognito. Everything behind that entry point runs in private networks across multiple Availability Zones, so the core platform is never directly exposed to the internet.

Inside that environment, Tamnoon combines two kinds of compute. Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) runs the always-on services behind the dashboard, while AWS Lambda powers the event-driven work of collecting findings, analyzing them, and executing remediations. A set of AWS messaging and workflow services, including Amazon EventBridge, Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS), and AWS Step Functions, coordinate these steps so large volumes of findings are processed reliably and in parallel, with no single bad record stalling the rest.

The AI layer runs on Amazon Bedrock. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model, gives Tamnoon’s agents a governed way to take action instead of open-ended access. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails then review both the request and the generated code before anything moves forward. Supporting services handle the rest of the platform: managed databases and caching for state, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) for playbooks and artifacts, and AWS Secrets Manager for credentials, so sensitive keys never live in application code.

On the customer side, everything to the left of the AWS Cloud boundary is what customers connect into Tamnoon. They can link their own AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud accounts, plug in the security tools their findings come from, and connect the destinations where they want outcomes delivered, such as Slack, Jira, ServiceNow, and GitHub.

Figure 2: Tamnoon AWS architecture

How Tamnoon maintains zero production issues

Zero production issues is a reality for Tamnoon’s customers, and it is no accident. Autonomy at Tamnoon sits inside a defense-in-depth safety architecture, where each layer assumes the one before it might miss something.

It starts before any fix is even drafted. No remediation is written until an independent safety assessment, focused on scope and deliberately biased toward caution, concludes that the change is safe to make. From there, the platform draws a hard line between reading and writing. Investigation steps are validated as strictly read-only, so the work of understanding a problem can never alter it. Only the remediation path is allowed to change anything, and every change it makes carries its own backup, verification, and rollback steps.

That discipline is reinforced by constant self-critique. Each generation step is paired with a reflection step that checks the output and feeds its critique back into regeneration, so the system is always reviewing its own work rather than trusting it outright. Those recommendations are also kept grounded in reality. Agent output is validated against automation results, user feedback, and training data drawn from real fixed alerts, and when the model cannot reach an accurate result on its own, a human is brought into the loop.

The final safeguard is at the moment of execution. The AI never holds cloud credentials. Instead, execution is brokered through short-lived, tenant-scoped credentials under customer-controlled trust, running in an isolated environment kept separate from the agents that plan the work. Wrapping all of this is human governance: remediations flow through an approval workflow with a full audit trail, and every AI capability is proven internally before it ever reaches a customer.

Data security and compliance

Tami reasons over sensitive customer data: alert payloads, resource identifiers, misconfigurations, and remediation context. That data must stay inside the AWS trust boundary, run with least privilege, and stay auditable. Standardizing on Amazon Bedrock makes that possible.

Sensitive content stays inside AWS

Every Tami workload invokes Anthropic Claude on Amazon Bedrock through the ChatBedrockConverse interface, rather than calling a third-party LLM endpoint. That single choice puts the full AI supply chain under one AWS native service, which has real consequences for how customer data is handled. Inference runs entirely within Tamnoon’s own AWS account in US commercial Regions, so data never leaves AWS. For information about model availability by Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock. Because Bedrock doesn’t retain or train on prompts or completions, customer data never reaches an external vendor in the first place.

That boundary holds even as workloads scale. Bedrock Cross-Region inference automatically routes requests to Regions within the US geographic boundary, increasing the throughput available to the application. The compute behind it stays private as well. Each service runs as an AWS Lambda function attached to a virtual private cloud (VPC), in private subnets with an explicit security group, no public ingress, and tightly controlled egress.

Guarding what reaches the model

Payloads can carry sensitive detail, so Tami applies Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to every request and response. The policy is enforced at the Bedrock layer, which means it covers all three services uniformly and no individual function’s prompt logic can bypass it. That single enforcement point does several things at once.

First, it protects sensitive data. PII and secret-like content is masked before it is ever persisted or surfaced, so nothing sensitive lingers where it doesn’t belong. It also guards against prompt injection, which matters because Tami reasons over untrusted findings that an unauthorized user could influence. Filtering at the guardrail layer stops a crafted payload from hijacking the model or exfiltrating context. Finally, denied topics and content filters keep the model’s output scoped to security remediation and nothing else. Every intervention is logged alongside AWS CloudTrail, giving enterprise customers a clear trail of governance evidence.

Least-privilege access

Access across the platform runs through a dedicated per-service IAM execution role, so each function can reach only what it needs and nothing more. That principle is easiest to see in how Tami touches Amazon Bedrock. Its only Bedrock permission is bedrock:InvokeModel, scoped to specific inference-profile and foundation-model ARNs. It has no ability to manage, train, or export models.

The same discipline extends to every other dependency. Access to AWS Secrets Manager is limited to the two secrets a function actually uses, SQS access is confined to its own input queue, and Amazon CloudWatch writes are restricted by namespace. There are no broad, catch-all roles anywhere in the design. Functions attach only to the managed AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole and AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole policies, and nothing wider than that.

Multi-tenant isolation and governance

Keeping tenants separated is a foundational requirement, and it is enforced from the very first call. Service-to-service calls use OAuth2 client credentials through Cognito, scoped per application, and work is processed one SQS message at a time with its tenant context attached. As a result, a single invocation only ever touches one tenant’s data.

Much of this assurance comes from treating the entire platform as code. IAM policies, network placement, model IDs, and alarms all live in versioned AWS CloudFormation and SAM templates, so every permission and model version is reviewable in source control with no manual console changes to drift out of sync. Model versions in particular are pinned to dated identifiers, for example claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929, which means a model change is always an explicit, reviewed code change rather than a silent upgrade.

That transparency carries through to runtime. Every inference call lands in AWS CloudTrail, attributable to the invoking role, and deterministic decoding with temperature set to zero keeps scoring and planning consistent from one run to the next. Failure handling is governed with the same rigor. Each service has an input queue with redrive, an error-handler function, a dead-letter queue, and CloudWatch alarms on timeouts and DLQ depth wired to on-call. Failures are contained and observable, and never silently dropped.

Results and impact

Tami has analyzed more than 14 million cloud alerts across Tamnoon’s customer base, a number tracked in Tamnoon’s 2026 State of Cloud Remediation report. The decisions Tami makes reflect patterns learned from these real-world environments.

For a typical customer, the results show up fast, usually within 90 days.

MetricBeforeAfter
Critical cloud exposureCompounds for months as alerts outpace headcountUp to 90% reduction in 90 days (source)
Remediation efficiencyThousands of raw alerts, no clear prioritizationUp to 100x efficiency through root-cause clustering (source)
Production issuesTeams avoid automation because of riskZero production issues across millions of workloads
Engineer timeHours per finding, repeated across backlog13,000+ hours saved per week across customer base (source)

The compression and zero-issue figures come from Tamnoon’s research. The pattern is consistent, showing fewer open exposures, far less manual work, and no downtime from the fixes themselves.

Conclusion

Building an agent that can reason about a cloud finding is the straightforward part. Building one you’d trust to act on production is the hard part. Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed service that provides access to high-performing foundation models along with the tooling to build agentic applications: orchestration, tool use, and guardrails, through a single API. That combination matters here for a specific reason: acting on production cloud infrastructure demands both strong reasoning and hard safety boundaries.

Four things make that possible:

  • Your exposures actually close: Tamnoon operates on live cloud infrastructure, not on tickets or workflow automation. The backlog goes down instead of sideways.
  • Autonomy scales without production risk: Every proposed action carries a confidence rating. SAFE actions can auto-execute while AWAITING DATA or RISKY actions pull in Tamnoon’s embedded cloud engineers.
  • Runs on the stack you already bought: Tamnoon works on top of popular CNAPPs and cloud security tooling. Every detection tool you already pay for starts paying off because its findings finally get closed.
  • Team capacity scales without growing: Fast, safe adoption of frontier AI means more exposures closed per analyst, with no added headcount.

Next steps

To get started with a similar architecture, consider the following:

  • Explore Amazon Bedrock and the models available through it.
  • Review the Amazon Bedrock documentation to plan your architecture.
  • Book a demo with Tamnoon to find out how much of your critical cloud exposure you can close in the next 90 days.

About the authors

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] Deploy and evaluate models with Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Deploy and evaluate models with Amazon SageMaker JumpStart

Choosing the right model for a specific application requires a practical way to test it with representative inputs. Amazon SageMaker JumpStart provides access to a broad catalog of already pretrained models. In this post, we show how to deploy an available model from SageMaker JumpStart, run a lightweight and repeatable performance test using the SageMaker Python SDK, and delete the endpoint when testing is complete. For supported models and available capacity, this workflow provides a repeatable evaluation path, although deployment time varies by model, instance type, quota, and AWS Region.

In 2026, SageMaker JumpStart introduced two improvements that simplify model discovery and deployment. In the Model Hub section of the Amazon SageMaker AI console, you can browse the SageMaker JumpStart catalog, view sample notebooks, and open them directly in SageMaker Studio. Pre-configured endpoint deployment options provide named configurations optimized for priorities such as low cost, low latency, or general-purpose workloads across a range of generative AI models, including Neuron-optimized configurations. Additionally, you can now go from Hugging Face model discovery to SageMaker AI deployment in a single click using the new deep link integration.

Solution overview

Our approach uses a reusable Python script that performs three steps:

  • Discover and deploy a model from SageMaker JumpStart.
  • Run model-specific sample prompts and measure latency, approximate output length, and single-request generation rate.
  • Clean up the endpoint.

This pattern works for many compatible SageMaker JumpStart models, although payload formats, required instance types, end-user license agreement (EULA) requirements, and response schemas may require model-specific adjustments.

Prerequisites

  • An AWS account with SageMaker AI permissions.
  • Python 3+ with SageMaker Python SDK v3 installed (pip install "sagemaker>=3,<4").
  • Sufficient GPU instance quota for the model you want to test or request a quota increase.

Step 1.a: Discover available models

UI path to find models in SageMaker JumpStart:

Figure 1: Browsing the model catalog on the SageMaker JumpStart Models page in SageMaker Studio

Code path using SageMaker Python SDK:

from sagemaker.core.jumpstart.notebook_utils import (
    list_jumpstart_models,
)

REGION = "us-east-1"

models = list_jumpstart_models(
    filter="task == textgeneration",
    region=REGION,
    list_versions=True,
)

print(f"Found {len(models)} text generation models")

for model_id, model_version in models[:10]:
    print(
        f" - {model_id} "
        f"(version {model_version})"
    )

Or search by model name:

from sagemaker.core.jumpstart.notebook_utils import list_jumpstart_models

ids = list_jumpstart_models(
    filter="model_id contains qwen",
    region=REGION,
    list_versions=True,
)

print(f"{len(ids)} models matched in {REGION}\n")

for model_id, version in ids:
    print(f"{model_id:<55} v{version}")

Step 1.b: Deploy the model

UI path to deploy models from SageMaker JumpStart:

Figure 2: Deploying a model from its SageMaker JumpStart detail page in SageMaker Studio

Code path using SageMaker Python SDK:

import time

from sagemaker.core.jumpstart.accessors import JumpStartModelsAccessor
from sagemaker.core.jumpstart.configs import JumpStartConfig
from sagemaker.core.training.configs import Compute
from sagemaker.serve import ModelBuilder

MODEL_ID = "huggingface-vlm-qwen3-5-27b"
MODEL_VERSION = "1.13.0"
REGION = "us-east-1"
ACCEPT_EULA = False  # Set True only after reviewing the model terms

def get_field(value, name, default=None):
    if isinstance(value, dict):
        return value.get(name, default)
    return getattr(value, name, default)

# Resolve the JumpStart-recommended deployment configuration.
specs = JumpStartModelsAccessor().get_model_specs(
    region=REGION,
    model_id=MODEL_ID,
    version=MODEL_VERSION,
)

if isinstance(specs, list):
    if not specs:
        raise ValueError(
            f"No JumpStart specification found for {MODEL_ID}"
        )
    specs = specs[0]

recommended_instance_type = get_field(
    specs,
    "default_inference_instance_type",
)

if not recommended_instance_type:
    raise ValueError(
        f"No recommended instance type found for {MODEL_ID}"
    )

print(f"Model: {MODEL_ID}")
print(f"Region: {REGION}")
print(f"Recommended instance: {recommended_instance_type}")

start = time.time()

jumpstart_config = JumpStartConfig(
    model_id=MODEL_ID,
    model_version=MODEL_VERSION,
    accept_eula=ACCEPT_EULA,
)

model_builder = ModelBuilder.from_jumpstart_config(
    jumpstart_config=jumpstart_config,
    compute=Compute(
        instance_type=recommended_instance_type,
        instance_count=1,
    ),
)

model = model_builder.build()
endpoint = model_builder.deploy()
deploy_time = time.time() - start

print(f"Deployed in {deploy_time:.1f} seconds")
print(f"Endpoint: {endpoint.endpoint_name}")

Step 2: Run sample prompts and measure performance

from sagemaker.core.payloads import retrieve_all_examples
import json
import time

MODEL_ID = "huggingface-vlm-qwen3-5-27b"
MODEL_VERSION = "1.13.0"
REGION = "us-east-1"

example_payloads = retrieve_all_examples(
    region=REGION,
    model_id=MODEL_ID,
    model_version=MODEL_VERSION,
    serialize=True,
)

#you can re-create the endpoint pointer using the endpoint name:
#from sagemaker.core.resources import Endpoint
#endpoint = Endpoint.get(endpoint_name="<your_endpoint_name>",region=REGION)

def read_response_body(result):
    body = result.body
    if hasattr(body, "read"):
        body = body.read()
    if isinstance(body, bytes):
        body = body.decode("utf-8")
    if isinstance(body, str):
        try:
            return json.loads(body)
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            return body
    return body

def extract_output(response):
    """Handle common JumpStart text-generation response formats."""
    if isinstance(response, list):
        response = response[0] if response else ""
    if isinstance(response, dict):
        choices = response.get("choices")
        if choices:
            choice = choices[0]
            message = choice.get("message")
            if isinstance(message, dict):
                return message.get("content", "")
            return choice.get("text", "")
        for field in (
            "generated_text",
            "output_text",
            "text",
        ):
            if field in response:
                return response[field]
    return response

results = []

for payload in example_payloads or []:
    start = time.perf_counter()
    result = endpoint.invoke(
        body=payload.body,
        content_type=payload.content_type,
        accept=payload.accept,
    )
    latency = time.perf_counter() - start
    response = read_response_body(result)
    output = extract_output(response)
    if not isinstance(output, str):
        output = json.dumps(output, indent=2)
    # This is an estimate based on whitespace-separated words.
    output_words = len(output.split())
    results.append(
        {
            "request_preview": payload.body[:50],
            "latency_s": round(latency, 2),
            "estimated_output_words": output_words,
            "words_per_second": round(
                output_words / latency,
                1,
            ) if latency > 0 else 0,
        }
    )
    print("Input:\n", payload.body, end="\n\n")
    print("Output:\n", output, end="\n\n")
    print(
        f"Latency: {latency:.2f} seconds\n"
        f"Estimated output words: {output_words}\n"
        f"Estimated single-request output generation rate: "
        f"{output_words / latency:.1f} words/second\n"
    )
    print("-" * 80)

print("\nSummary:")
for result in results:
    print(result)

Result:

Input:
{"max_tokens": 256, "messages": [{"content": "What is deep learning?", "role": "user"}], "model": "/opt/ml/model"}
Output:
Here's a thinking process that leads to the explanation of deep learning:
1. **Deconstruct the Request:**
* **Question:** "What is deep learning?"
* **Intent:** The user wants a clear, comprehensive, yet accessible definition and overview of deep learning.
* **Target Audience:** Likely someone looking for a general understanding, possibly a student, tech
enthusiast, or professional exploring the field. The tone should be informative, structured, and
not overly jargon-heavy (though key terms need explanation).
2. **Initial Brainstorming & Key Concepts:**
* What is it? A subset of machine learning, which is a subset of AI.
* Core mechanism: Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs).
* "Deep" means many layers (hidden layers).
* How does it work? Learning representations from data (feature learning).
* Key applications: Image recognition, NLP, speech, self-driving cars.
* Why is it popular now? Big data, GPU power, better algorithms.
* Pros/Cons: High accuracy vs. black box, data hunger.
3. **Structuring the Answer:**
Latency: 9.07 seconds
Estimated output words: 153
Estimated single-request output generation rate: 16.9 words/second
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary:
{'request_preview': '{"max_tokens": 256, "messages": {"content": "What', 'latency_s': 9.07, 'estimated_output_words': 153, 'words_per_second': 16.9}

Step 3: Cleanup

print(f"Deleting endpoint: {endpoint.endpoint_name}")
endpoint.delete()
endpoint.wait_for_delete()
print("Endpoint deleted")

Conclusion

This pattern works for many available SageMaker JumpStart models, but the payload format, required instance type, EULA, and response parsing may require model-specific adjustments. By using consistent test prompts and measuring latency, throughput, and output quality across models, you can compare options and select the right fit for your workload.

Try this approach with different models from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart to find the right balance of quality, speed, and cost for your applications.

References

  • SageMaker Python SDK Documentation
  • Benchmark and Optimize SageMaker JumpStart Deployment (blog post)
  • From Hugging Face to SageMaker Studio in One Click (blog post)
  • Amazon SageMaker JumpStart

About the authors

item.title: [DeepInfra] Western Open-Weight Models: Beam and Le Chonk
item.content:encoded:
Western Open-Weight Models: Beam and Le Chonk

Published on 2026.10.14 by Stefan Fidanov

Reflection AI and Mistral shipped open-weight flagships a day apart in the first week of October, and both say they compare to the best China has to offer.

Reflection’s Beam is a 501B-parameter workhorse that claims GLM-5.2-level reasoning, a bar Z.ai has already raised with GLM-5.3, on a fraction of the inference compute. Mistral’s Large 4, which the company nicknamed “le Chonk,” is a 1-trillion-parameter flagship built, trained, and served in Europe.

Chinese labs still set the bar on price per capability, and neither launch moves it. On Artificial Analysis’s open-weights index, Le Chonk scores 38 against 46 for MiMo-V2.6-Pro and 45 for GLM-5.3.

So the Western pitch rests on four other questions: where the model runs, who operates it, which license applies, and what each answer costs. Let’s explore this in more detail.

At A Glance: Beam, Le Chonk, And The Bar They’re Chasing

Here’s each launch next to its named Chinese rivals and the strongest US open model in production. Beam and Le Chonk rows are launch-day promises.

ModelOriginTotal / active paramsLicenseWeightsWhere you can run it today (prices: DeepInfra)
Reflection BeamUS501B / 23BApache 2.0 (promised)“Later this month”Waitlist API at Reflection
Mistral Large 4 (le Chonk)France1.05T / 49BNot yet namedEnd of OctoberMistral Studio preview, $1.36 / $4.18 per 1M
GLM-5.3China753B / ~40BCustom GLM-5.3 LicensePublicDeepInfra, $0.90 / $4.00 per 1M
Kimi K3China2.8T / 104BKimi K3 LicensePublicDeepInfra, $2.85 / $14.25 per 1M
DeepSeek V4.1 FlashChina552B / 16BMITPublicDeepInfra, $0.20 / $0.60 per 1M
InklingUS975B / 41BApache 2.0PublicDeepInfra, $0.95 / $4.05 per 1M

The Price-Per-Capability Bar Chinese Labs Set

For the last year and a half, the open-weight frontier has been Chinese. Nathan Lambert’s Interconnects dates the clear Chinese lead to around April 2025, and Hugging Face’s summer 2026 state of open models found that this year’s releases above 100B parameters were built on Chinese models or used Chinese-lab artifacts.

Chinese labs also paired strong models with aggressive pricing. On Artificial Analysis’s open-weights leaderboard (Intelligence Index v4.3.2), MiMo-V2.6-Pro scores 46, GLM-5.3 scores 45, Kimi K3 scores 44, and GLM-5.3-Flash scores 42. The best US entries on that leaderboard are Inkling at 25 and Nemotron 3 Ultra at 23. Le Chonk lands at 38 on its own Artificial Analysis page, and AA’s launch analysis calls it the “most intelligent model from outside the US and China.”

Here they are against output price.

The upper-left corner belongs to China. GLM-5.3-Flash scores 42 at $0.50 per million output tokens on DeepInfra, and the Western models score lower at higher prices. Beam is missing because it has no data on either axis yet. Artificial Analysis hasn’t scored it, and Reflection hasn’t published pricing. On benchmark per dollar alone, it’s easy to see why both labs chose to argue about something else. (We covered the broader open vs closed version of this trade-off separately.)

Beam: A Workhorse Sold On Compute Per Answer

Reflection’s launch post concedes that Kimi K3 remains ahead on raw capability, so it sells Beam on efficiency instead. Beam, it says, “achieves scores comparable to GLM-5.2 while using 3–4× less inference compute.” Beam is a text-only mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 501B total parameters and 23B active per token, pretrained on 23.8T tokens across 6,144 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs.

Read the footnote before you quote that number. Reflection defines generation compute as roughly 2 × active parameters × mean generated tokens per attempt, counting reasoning plus the final answer. That makes it an estimate, and its first factor is easy to chart:

Beam’s 23B active parameters (highlighted) against GLM-5.2’s roughly 40B give it about a 1.7x edge per token. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM-5.3-Flash are leaner still. To reach 3-4x, the remainder has to come from Beam generating fewer tokens per answer. Artificial Analysis, which had early access, said Beam looks like “one of the most token-efficient open models we’ve seen for its level of intelligence.” Here’s the arithmetic:

def decode_flops(active_params_b: float, generated_tokens: int) -> float:
    """Reflection's proxy: 2 x active params x generated tokens (decode only)."""
    return 2 * active_params_b * 1e9 * generated_tokens

# Active parameters, in billions
BEAM, GLM_5_2 = 23, 40

param_ratio = GLM_5_2 / BEAM
print(f"Per-token advantage from active params: {param_ratio:.2f}x")

# What token ratio would close the gap to Reflection's 3-4x claim?
for claimed in (3.0, 4.0):
    implied = claimed / param_ratio
    print(f"{claimed:.0f}x total implies GLM-5.2 writes {implied:.2f}x more tokens per answer")

# Sanity check with a hypothetical 6,000-token reasoning trace
print(f"Beam, 6k tokens: {decode_flops(BEAM, 6_000) / 1e12:.0f} TFLOPs")copy

So GLM-5.2 would need to write roughly 1.7x to 2.3x more output tokens for the same result. Does Beam actually reason that briefly? That’s unverified until the weights ship and independent evaluators measure its output length. Once it’s callable, test the claim on your own prompts. The formula also leaves out the costs that dominate agent workloads.

Prefill is the big one. An agent loop that re-reads a 100K-token context on every tool call spends most of its compute reading, and the 3-4x number says nothing about that phase. All 501B parameters also have to sit in GPU memory even though only 23B fire per token. Cost per finished task tracks turns and tokens more than per-token price, as we argued in small open-weight models’ hidden cost advantage.

Le Chonk: A Flagship Sold On Where It Runs

Mistral went the other way. Mistral Large 4 is a 1.05T-parameter MoE with 49B active per token (52B if you count embeddings and output layers, per its Hugging Face card). It takes text and image input across more than 160 languages, and Mistral says it significantly outperforms “any open-weight model developed in the US or Europe.” On specs, plan around what is served, not what is printed: Mistral’s docs list a 1M-token context window, but Artificial Analysis lists roughly 512K for the preview API it tested, and Beam’s beta API caps requests at 256K against a claimed 1M.

The headline is jurisdiction. Mistral says Large 4 was trained from scratch on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in its own European datacenters, and the preview is served on the same hardware. It will run in “a European deployment that Mistral operates end-to-end, independently of other digital service providers and under European law,” and for security work it can run on private cloud or on-premise. Guillaume Lample put the reasoning bluntly to WIRED: “If you use a closed model, there is no guarantee it will still be there tomorrow.”

Think of it as a ladder, where each rung moves the model closer to hardware you control.

Today Le Chonk sits on the bottom two rungs, and the top two depend on a license Mistral hasn’t named. The capability is real but . Artificial Analysis measured $1.13 per Intelligence Index task at list price, more than 4x what higher-scored open models like GLM-5.3-Flash cost, partly because Large 4 produced 200M output tokens to finish the index against a median of 82M. The data sovereignty case for open weights only pays off once you can actually climb the ladder. Both launches also lack independent serving numbers. No measured latency, throughput, or time to first token under load exists for Beam or Large 4, so the ladder assesses where a model can run; how well it serves stays unknown until weights ship and providers publish measurements.

Reading The Scoreboard

Both launch posts carry vendor-reported benchmarks. Reflection’s is more complete, and it includes competitors its headline skips. Below is a subset of Reflection’s published numbers as of October 8 (Beam’s scores were revised that day). Competitor scores are Reflection’s compilation from third-party leaderboards, so read the table as claimed scores against the baselines Reflection chose. Bold marks the row leader, and NR means not reported.

BenchmarkBeamInklingNemotron 3 UltraGLM-5.2GLM-5.3Kimi K3DeepSeek V4.1 Flash
Terminal Bench v2.180.163.856.481.088.288.390.6
DeepSWE v1.144.4NRNR44.061.068.074.2
SWE Bench Pro v165.554.346.462.1NRNRNR
HLE (no tools)36.229.726.740.542.346.939.1
GPQA Diamond90.587.287.091.291.793.590.9
MCP Atlas78.776.063.177.884.282.3NR

Source: reflection.ai/beam, all scores vendor-reported.

Within that chosen set, Beam beats the two US models, Inkling and Nemotron 3 Ultra, on every shared row, and those are also the table’s two weakest models. GLM-5.2, the model in Reflection’s headline, is no longer Z.ai’s flagship. GLM-5.3 shipped in late August and leads Beam on every row where both report. Mistral reports Large 4 at 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, level with the 61.0 Reflection’s table prints for GLM-5.3, but VentureBeat points out that the live leaderboard has Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3 nearer 69%. Treat both vendors’ tables as dated snapshots of a moving leaderboard. For more on the Chinese side, see our Kimi K3 vs DeepSeek V4 Pro vs GLM-5.2 comparison.

Le Chonk’s numbers live on a different scoreboard, since what exists for it is Mistral’s own claims plus Artificial Analysis’s independent measurements:

Le Chonk measureValue
Intelligence Index v4.3.238
DeepSWE v1.1 (Mistral-reported)61.7%
DeepSWE v1.1 (live leaderboard: Kimi K3, GLM-5.3)~69%
Cost per Index task at list price$1.13
Output tokens to finish the Index200M (median model: 82M)

Sources: Artificial Analysis’s model page and launch analysis, Mistral’s launch post, VentureBeat. Read the two tables together and the picture is the same from both launches: neither Western flagship beats GLM-5.3 on a scale anyone else can check.

The Rest Of The Western Open-Weight Bench

Several other Western options are deployable today. None matches GLM-5.3 on capability, but several win on license and price.

ModelLabTotal / activeLicenseAA Index v4.3.2DeepInfra $/1M in / outBest role
InklingThinking Machines (US)975B / 41BApache 2.025$0.95 / $4.05Multimodal agents (text, image, audio in)
Nemotron 3 UltraNVIDIA (US)550B / 55BOpenMDW 1.123$0.50 / $2.20Reasoning where open data and recipe matter
Nemotron 3 SuperNVIDIA (US)120B / 12BNVIDIA Nemotron Open Model LicenseNot listed$0.085 / $0.40Cheap agent steps
gpt-oss-120bOpenAI (US)117B / 5.1BApache 2.0Not listed$0.037 / $0.17Classification, routing, bulk extraction
Gemma 4 31BGoogle (US)31B denseApache 2.0Not listed$0.20 / $0.40Small-footprint self-hosting

Inkling is the closest thing to a Western Beam that you can call right now. It’s a 975B MoE under Apache 2.0, and it accepts audio, which neither Beam nor Le Chonk does. Nemotron 3 Ultra’s selling point is openness beyond the weights, since NVIDIA released training data and recipes alongside the checkpoints. At the cheap end, gpt-oss-120b and Nemotron 3 Super are the grunt-work picks. At $0.17 and $0.40 per million output tokens, frontier capability stops mattering for triage and routing steps.

Licensing Is Where Western Open-Weight Models Can Win

Scan the license columns and the Chinese flagships are drifting toward custom terms. GLM-5.2 shipped under plain MIT, but GLM-5.3 moved to its own license, which requires companies above $10B in revenue to pass Z.ai’s security review before offering it as a hosted service. Kimi K3 and Qwen3.8-Max ship under their own named licenses with commercial conditions. DeepSeek is the holdout, still on MIT.

The Western side is moving the other way, at least at Reflection. Beam’s weights are promised under Apache 2.0, which matches Inkling, gpt-oss-120b, and Gemma 4. That’s the license legal teams approve without a meeting. Mistral is the open question. Its previous flagship, Mistral Large 3, was Apache 2.0, but its most recent mid-size release, Medium 3.5, uses a modified MIT license that excludes companies with more than $20M in monthly revenue. Large 4’s Hugging Face page has no license field at all.

Axios also notes that the FY2026 NDAA directs the Defense Department to remove DeepSeek from government and contractor systems, and that Western releases give businesses alternatives to Chinese options they may have eschewed for security reasons. Reflection CEO Misha Laskin told Axios: “Once you’re spending that amount on intelligence, you want to move from renting it to owning it yourself.”

Three different risks hide inside the word “origin”.

  • Serving location is whose datacenter processes your prompts: every model you can call on DeepInfra today, Chinese-origin or not, runs in US data centers with zero retention, which covers most data-handling concerns.
  • Weights origin is who built the model and what its license permits, which drives legal exposure and what you can change.
  • Statutory procurement is the narrowest case and the only one where origin is disqualifying by itself: if the NDAA or a customer contract excludes Chinese-origin weights, no amount of US serving changes that, and Beam, Le Chonk, Inkling, Nemotron, and gpt-oss are your choices.

If statutory procurement isn’t your situation, the Chinese flagships earn their place on price per capability. The same split answers the obvious question about Le Chonk: if you need it under European law specifically, that path runs through Mistral’s own EU deployment or self-hosting once the weights ship; a US inference provider can’t offer European jurisdiction.

Running Western Open-Weight Models On Deepinfra Today

You don’t need to wait for either launch to build the plumbing. Make model choice a policy decision in code, so origin and license sit next to price in one place. DeepInfra serves a huge collection of models through one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so the policy is just a list of model IDs.

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ["DEEPINFRA_API_TOKEN"],
    base_url="https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai",
)

# Candidates per role, tagged with origin and license.
# Add Beam or Mistral Large 4 here once a provider serves their weights.
CATALOG = {
    "agent": [
        ("thinkingmachines/Inkling", "US", "apache-2.0"),
        ("nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B", "US", "openmdw-1.1"),
        ("zai-org/GLM-5.3", "CN", "glm-5.3"),
    ],
    "triage": [
        ("openai/gpt-oss-120b", "US", "apache-2.0"),
        ("deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash", "CN", "mit"),
    ],
}

POLICY = {"origins": {"US", "EU"}, "licenses": {"apache-2.0", "openmdw-1.1", "mit"}}


def allowed(role: str) -> list[str]:
    return [
        model for model, origin, license_id in CATALOG[role]
        if origin in POLICY["origins"] and license_id in POLICY["licenses"]
    ]


def complete(role: str, messages: list[dict]) -> str:
    last_error = None
    for model in allowed(role):  # first allowed model wins, the rest are fallbacks
        try:
            resp = client.chat.completions.create(model=model, messages=messages, timeout=60)
            return resp.choices[0].message.content
        except Exception as err:
            last_error = err
    raise RuntimeError(f"No allowed model succeeded for role {role!r}") from last_error


print(complete("triage", [{"role": "user", "content": "Classify: 'refund not received'"}]))copy

Loosen POLICY and GLM-5.3 joins the agent pool. When Beam’s weights land, it’s one more tuple.

Next, build a token-efficiency check, since Beam’s argument rests on generated tokens per answer. Run one prompt set across candidates and record what each wrote:

import asyncio
import os
from openai import AsyncOpenAI

client = AsyncOpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ["DEEPINFRA_API_TOKEN"],
    base_url="https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai",
)

# (model id, active params in billions, $ per 1M input, $ per 1M output)
CANDIDATES = [
    ("thinkingmachines/Inkling", 41, 0.95, 4.05),
    ("nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B", 55, 0.50, 2.20),
    ("zai-org/GLM-5.3", 40, 0.90, 4.00),
]

PROMPT = [{"role": "user", "content": "Find the bug: def avg(xs): return sum(xs) / len(xs) - 1"}]


async def measure(model: str, active_b: float, price_in: float, price_out: float) -> dict:
    resp = await client.chat.completions.create(model=model, messages=PROMPT)
    u = resp.usage
    return {
        "model": model.split("/")[-1],
        "out_tokens": u.completion_tokens,
        "decode_tflops": 2 * active_b * 1e9 * u.completion_tokens / 1e12,
        "cost_usd": (u.prompt_tokens * price_in + u.completion_tokens * price_out) / 1e6,
    }


async def main():
    rows = await asyncio.gather(*(measure(*c) for c in CANDIDATES))
    for r in sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r["cost_usd"]):
        print(f"{r['model']:<40} {r['out_tokens']:>6} tok  {r['decode_tflops']:>7.1f} TFLOPs  ${r['cost_usd']:.5f}")


asyncio.run(main())copy

Run it over a few hundred real prompts and you get Reflection’s proxy, measured on your workload. When Beam is callable, add a row and see whether the 3-4x survives contact with your traffic.

Everything here runs on DeepInfra’s pay-as-you-go pricing with no contract, on zero-retention US infrastructure with SOC 2 and ISO 27001 certification.

Conclusion

Neither Beam nor Le Chonk closes the gap with the best Chinese open models. Reflection’s own table shows that, and so does Artificial Analysis. They change the terms of the comparison instead. The split is almost tidy: Beam, sold on writing fewer tokens per answer, argues compute per answer and an Apache 2.0 license, while Le Chonk, which burned 200M output tokens finishing Artificial Analysis’s index, argues European operation and on-prem control. Inkling, the Nemotron 3 models, and gpt-oss-120b are already competing on permissive licensing and price. If your procurement rules exclude Chinese-origin weights, that’s a real menu for the first time, and it grows when the weights land.

Start with the models you can run today on DeepInfra’s model catalog, wire up the routing policy, and the new Western open-weight models become one-line additions. Questions about any of these models? Reach us at feedback@deepinfra.com, join our Discord, or find us on X at @DeepInfra.

FAQ

Is Reflection Beam available on DeepInfra?

Not yet. As of launch, Beam was available only through a waitlist beta on Reflection’s own OpenAI-compatible API, and its Hugging Face organization had no public models. Reflection has promised Apache 2.0 weights later in October, and inference providers can host the model once those ship. Until then, the closest Western MoE on DeepInfra is Inkling.

When will Mistral Large 4 weights be released, and under what license?

Mistral says by the end of October, and its Hugging Face page lists an October 31 ETA. Mistral hasn’t announced a license, and its recent releases don’t settle the question, so check the LICENSE file before planning a self-hosted deployment.

Is Beam actually 3-4x cheaper to run than GLM-5.2?

Not necessarily in dollars. The 3-4x figure estimates decode compute alone, and Reflection hasn’t published pricing, so dollar cost is unknown. The token-efficiency check in the code section above measures it on your traffic.

item.title: [AI21 Labs] The hidden mismatch: Evaluating coding agents on the work de…
item.description: Full title: The hidden mismatch: Evaluating coding agents on the work developers actually do
item.content:encoded:
In brief

We’ve all heard it before: your AI system – whether an agent, harness, or routing layer – is only as good as the evaluation behind it.

We’ve also heard: public benchmarks are poor proxies for real developer traffic. In terms of what they ask for, how they phrase it, task difficulty, and how trajectories unfold over the session.

We saw this discrepancy up close when we surveyed our internal developer traffic. The results challenged our assumptions about agentic coding tasks, and we used these lessons to build a robust benchmark that preserves quality on real-world coding tasks in our intelligent gateway. This post covers that journey.

The real distribution of developer work

Luckily, to understand the gap between public benchmarks and real usage, we have the benefit of real live data from our internal team of developers. To make sense of this traffic, we developed an internal coding task classifier and ran seven weeks of real developer traffic through it.

What we saw when we looked at the resulting task distribution completely challenged our intuition about agentic coding habits:

FIGURE 1. Top-level categories were derived from the data, and subcategories were derived inside each category. Total of 15 categories, 84 subcategories, and 4,211 turns.

If you look at the tasks measured by a standard benchmark like SWE-bench, it would seem that developers use agents primarily for pure code generation and fixing bugs from a clean slate. But our classifier revealed a totally different reality.

Lessons from seven weeks of real-world developer traffic

Developers use agents as thought partners, not just as code generators. In our traffic, only about 11% of real developer turns ask the agent to write code. The vast majority of the time, developers are asking clarifying questions, pasting context, doing analysis, or requesting reviews. The single most common message we see is a clarifying question.

Interactive workflows vs. single-turn tasks. The data shows that developer-agent interactions are highly conversational. Developers aren’t just dropping a 1,000-word GitHub issue into a chat and walking away. They are typing short, 80-character messages mid-session. They are debugging step-by-step, pasting console logs, and iterating on the agent’s output.

Where real-world developer traffic and public benchmarks diverge

Task type

We ran several public benchmarks (including SWE-bench, HumanEval, and Spider) through this same classifier to build out our comparison. The mismatch with our internal data was glaring. Almost all of these public benchmarks focus on writing code from scratch or fixing a bug to pass a test.

FIGURE 2. The same categories applied to real usage and to 23 benchmarks. Number in cell reflects % of a dataset’s message. Confirmations, redirections, git commands and pasted context make up about 40% of real user turns, yet appear in no coding benchmark. Despite the fact that confirmations, redirections, git commands, and pasted context make up about 40% of real developer turns, these interactive properties and context-sharing behaviors appear in almost no public coding benchmarks.

Task difficulty

Beyond not covering real types of coding work, public benchmarks also fail to accurately reflect task difficulty. Standard evaluation sets often test deep, architectural knowledge of a codebase’s internals. But in the real world? A developer is much more likely to ask a quick, practical question like, “Why do I not see my changes in git status?”

Because benchmarks over-index on these highly complex, multi-file architectural issues, they give us a skewed sense of what models actually need to do and can therefore make smaller or cheaper models look artificially incapable of handling everyday traffic. You can see this in the comparison below between the median turn count across tasks from real developer sessions versus a frontier model tested on our benchmark:

FIGURE 3. Median turn count across task categories, as compared between real developer sessions and data generated from running Claude Opus 5.5 on our benchmark.

Task context

We found another major difference between real-world and public benchmark traffic: context. A typical benchmark task is presented as a well-written,1,000-character GitHub issue on a clean code checkout.

But real developer messages are messy. Averaging around 80 characters, they arrive right in the middle of an active session, stacked on top of an extensive history of conversation, tool outputs, and half-finished file changes. Over 60% of our internal sessions contain more than one distinct task. If you evaluate an agent solely on how it handles a single, well-scoped prompt from a pristine start, you are ignoring the reality of mid-session context switching.

Building a real-world benchmark

Defining the goal

Proving the discrepancy between public benchmarks and real-world developer traffic was the easy part. Now, we had to build a new benchmark that would resolve the gap.

The ideal evaluation would simply use our own developers’ real workflows. But building a natural task distribution creates an immediate tug-of-war between three competing properties: drawn from real work, context-rich, and capable of being graded automatically.

Real developer sessions meet the first two criteria, but are almost impossible to grade automatically. There is no pre-written test suite or rubric for a developer asking, “Why is my database connection dropping on line 42?” The intent lives entirely in the developer’s head, making it hard to measure if an agent succeeded without human review. On the other hand, public benchmarks are perfectly runnable and easy to grade automatically, but as we saw earlier, they lack relevance to real-world context.

Our goal was to collapse the tradeoff: combine the automated gradability of public benchmark tasks with the messy reality of actual traffic. We built a new benchmark, guided by four principles:

1. Let real traffic set the quotas. Instead of randomly sampling public tasks, we used the insights from our internal classifier to set quotas. If 40% of our real traffic consisted of clarifying questions and codebase analysis, then 40% of our benchmark needed to test exactly that.

2. Mix public tasks with internal code. Public tasks can’t cover your internal libraries, custom environments, or company conventions. To make the benchmark realistic, we mined our own internal repositories for tasks that had already been solved and merged. We verified that these internal tasks could be graded by our own test suites, and then added them to the pool alongside public tasks. That process looks something like this:

FIGURE 4. Mining GitHub and public benchmark tasks to create a comprehensive benchmark that covers expected real-world coding habits.

Synthesizing from traces involves analyzing real user interaction logs and session recordings to recreate realistic developer tasks and multi-turn scenarios.

3. Write like a developer. A 1,000-word, perfectly formatted bug report doesn’t test an agent’s ability to understand the short, 80-character, often ambiguous messages that our developers actually type. We changed the wrapper, but kept the underlying code environment and automated tests identical.

4. Start in the middle. Finally, because developers rarely ask for code from a clean start, an evaluation must eventually account for history. We built internal replay infrastructure that allows us to restore a real developer session at any point in its trajectory, complete with the accumulated context and modified files. By simulating the developer’s next move from the middle of a messy session, we get the truest measure of how an agent will actually perform in the wild.

By carefully selecting tasks that matched our true category mix, rewriting the prompts to sound like real developers, and blending in our own codebase, we created a 613-task benchmark that mirrors reality.

Then we put our benchmark to the ultimate test: measuring the quality of traffic flowing through our intelligent Gateway.

Does it hold up? Stress-testing our real-world coding benchmark

To test how well our benchmark captures the natural distribution of real-world coding tasks compared to public benchmarks, we wanted to see how a popular frontier model behaves on real user sessions versus each of these two benchmarks. For that test, we turned to the frontier-powered router in our intelligent Gateway, which sits between our developers and foundation models and has been trained for agentic coding traffic. Every time a developer sends a message, the Gateway’s router scores the task difficulty to make a split-second decision: Does this request require our most expensive, highly capable premium model, or can a cheaper, faster model handle it just fine?

This router can be tuned to route an expected percentage of traffic to the premium model, allowing us to trade off cost and quality. We reasoned that we’d know if we succeeded in building a truly representative benchmark if the shape of how the Gateway routes requests is consistent between real user sessions and our benchmark.

We measure that shape by looking at the premium routing threshold: the percentage of tasks the Gateway sends to the premium model. We set that target number at 25% and compared how the routing percentage correlates across live developer traffic and different benchmarks:

Test #1: Measuring our Gateway’s live traffic against a public benchmark (green line). Deployed on real incoming traffic, the Gateway misjudged the traffic and ended up sending nearly 50% of the requests to the premium model, overstepping its target budget by 23 points.

Test #2: Measuring our Gateway’s live traffic with our benchmark. Showing a striking correlation with our natural coding data, the Gateway landed just 0.5 points away from its target budget. This demonstrates that we have not only matched the task distribution of our real user sessions, but that the Gateway also successfully routed hard tasks to the premium model at the same rate in both cases.

FIGURE 5. The Gateway’s router threshold was set on its own data to send a target share of tasks to the premium model (x-axis), then applied unchanged to 1,905 real developer messages from our Gateway (y-axis).

Because the router was finally evaluated on a distribution that matched actual coding habits, it didn’t just save money; it proved that it could correctly identify when to rely on a cheaper model for a simple git question, and when to bring in the heavy hitter for a complex feature request.

What this means for your team

Ultimately, whether you are building a router, tuning a prompt, or choosing a model for your organization, your results will only ever be as accurate as your evaluation. If you want to know how a coding agent will perform in the wild, that’s where you have to measure it.

Here are the core takeaways for any team evaluating coding agents:

  • Measure your traffic before you choose a benchmark. If 90% of your team’s requests are codebase questions and bug triage, testing your agents on a benchmark made entirely of code-generation tasks will lead you astray.
  • Match the mix, the difficulty, and the language. Rewriting prompts or re-weighting tasks alone isn’t enough to transfer to real life. You have to combine them, and ideally, introduce tasks mined from your own private codebases.
  • Price sessions, not single tasks. Because developers work conversationally, model switching inside a session costs real money and context tokens. Only a session-level evaluation can see that true cost.
  • Test decisions, not just scores. A benchmark score doesn’t matter in a vacuum. An evaluation is only trustworthy when a model choice, a routing policy, or a budget threshold set on it actually holds up on real, live traffic

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] Uber's CISO on building an insider threat program for AI
item.content:encoded:
Uber runs one of the world's largest real-time marketplaces, with over 40 million trips and delivery orders a day. Philip Martin, Uber's Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), leads the team that protects Uber's data and the riders, drivers, and couriers who use the platform in the real world. His team started working with Claude on threat modeling before Claude Code existed, assembling context by hand. Now, with Claude Fable, Claude gathers that context itself from code, design docs, and ticket history.

Martin thinks AI agents need the same kind of insider threat program companies already run for their employees. We spoke with him about that idea, why he thinks so much about accidental misuse, and how Uber's open-source monitoring tools work alongside Enterprise Frontier Safeguards.

How are frontier models changing your security team’s work?

The really big difference between prior models and today’s frontier models is their ability to incorporate additional context over long time horizons, and as a result, generate really specific outputs. When we're doing security reviews or threat modeling for a given service application, we can let the models consume a lot more context about the service, whether that's the code itself, design documents, issues in Jira, or historical context on what the service is supposed to do and what it interacts with.

I see the same thing emerging with teams of agents. I can imagine a world in the not-too-distant future where each service has an agent associated with it that understands that service very well, and those agents can talk to each other, the same way the services might in production, about the threat model: this is my threat model, this is where my data comes from. That team-of-agents effect will take us to the next level of efficacy.

Uber worked with our team Enterprise Frontier Safeguards. Why was this important for Uber?

One thing Anthropic and Uber have in common is a bone-deep focus on safety, albeit in very different contexts. When Uber thinks about safety, we think about rider safety, protecting personal data. Anthropic wants to prevent the misuse of its frontier models, but Uber needs to protect our customer data, our trade secrets, and any other proprietary information. Enterprise Frontier Safeguards allow us to strike this balance: the safeguards are in place, but our data is not accessible to Anthropic without our permission.

It gives us control of our data and control of the risk mitigation and the actions we decide to take after a safeguard is triggered. I think we share a responsibility to make sure these models are used safely and effectively in the world.

When your team walked us through the design, it was clear that you heard our feedback. You put us in the driver's seat. This allows us to protect our data while still being responsible stewards of the capabilities of these models.

How Enterprise Frontier Safeguards fit with the safety monitoring you already run on AI deployments Uber?

We've done a ton of work since the very beginning on how we deploy AI safely within Uber. We recently open-sourced a product called AI Detection and Response (ADR) (opens in new tab), designed to gather real-time telemetry and take real-time action in the agent harnesses we deploy.

It complements Anthropic's safeguards, because we now have access to enhanced data to detect when an agent is acting outside its bounds and respond in real time. We have our own view of what's going on, plus output from Anthropic's classifier, and we can integrate both into our overall detection environment, much like a traditional cybersecurity one. It's all about assembling context effectively to reach a decision as fast, and with as much certainty, as possible.

I think we'll see Enterprise Frontier Safeguards feed into ADR as a data source. Together with our LLM gateway, which builds a perimeter and controls how AI is used within Uber, those make up our overall AI security architecture.

Where do you think defenders should prioritize their focus next when it comes to securing AI systems?

Number one is real-time detection and intervention: getting as close as we can to the human entering a prompt in a harness, to be able to tell them, "You probably don't want to do that," or "The tool this model is about to call, the place it's about to connect to, is probably not something you want to happen."

Number two is better understanding emerging patterns. We look at trends in model behavior and detect new behaviors we didn't know were possible. That becomes a cycle. We look at the data, in many cases with the assistance of LLMs, discover these behaviors as they appear, and build safeguards against them back into the real-time platform. Then new behaviors emerge, because constraints create new behaviors, and we find those too.

What would you tell other leaders who are hesitant about the monitoring frontier models require?

AI adoption is a business imperative. It's coming whether we want it or not, and it's going to bring real benefits to businesses and people around the world. But there's also real potential for harm, and the stakes rise as models get more capable and take on more complex, autonomous work.

Every company already runs an insider threat program for its people. Nobody argues about that. We accept the sometimes onerous data retention, and we monitor things we'd rather not monitor, because we know humans occasionally act outside the bounds of their role, for any number of reasons.

Frontier models introduce the same risk. These models may be directed to act outside the constraints we expect them to operate within. So we need the equivalent capability for AI. That insider threat program for models is going to be essential to rolling these systems out safely and securely.

Learn more about Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (opens in new tab).

LiquidAI

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

  • Best-in-class agent: Competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on agentic and tool-use tasks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19.
  • Reasoning at MoE speed: Always thinks before it answers. With only 2B active parameters per token, each reasoning token is cheap.
  • Efficient inference: 184 tok/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tok/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU.

How we built a reasoning agent with 2B active parameters

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:

  • Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
  • Teacher specialization
  • Multi-domain on-policy distillation (MOPD), non-agentic: distill the specialist teachers on non-agentic tasks.
  • MOPD, agentic: a second distillation stage focused on agentic tasks.
  • Agentic reinforcement learning (Agentic RL): train the model inside agent harnesses, such as OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenCode.

Benchmark results

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

BenchmarkLFM2.5-24B-A2BQwen3.6-35B-A3BGemma-4-26B-A4B-itNemotron-3.5-Lightning (30B-A3B)
AutomationBench27.698.725.462.61
BFCLv465.0165.0057.0953.78
ToolSandbox80.7175.0272.0975.13
LiveClaw48.0938.1941.2537.72
PinchBench83.1889.9377.1284.20
τ³-Bench Banking8.047.634.547.01
WebArena Verified26.7537.6225.6228.69
GPQA Diamond74.4283.6974.9072.42
AA-Omniscience-24.90-24.35-59.39-3.58
HLE7.407.698.575.65
IFEval96.7593.0692.0094.19
IFBench74.6964.2147.4471.67
Multi-IF84.3881.5382.1982.34
MATH-50096.0496.7395.6696.40
SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode)51.0066.2025.8053.40
SciCode32.7137.3535.4227.78

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Inference speed on CPU and GPU

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

How to use LFM2.5-24B-A2B

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):

pip install -U transformers

Then load and run the model:

from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, TextStreamer

model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B"
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    device_map="auto",
    dtype="bfloat16",
#   attn_implementation="flash_attention_2" <- uncomment on compatible GPU
)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
streamer = TextStreamer(tokenizer, skip_prompt=True, skip_special_tokens=True)

prompt = "What is C. elegans?"

input_ids = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
    tokenize=True,
)["input_ids"].to(model.device)

output = model.generate(
    input_ids,
    do_sample=True,
    temperature=0.1,
    top_k=50,
    repetition_penalty=1.05,
    max_new_tokens=512,
    streamer=streamer,
)

Use it in your agent harness

Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:

hermes config set model.provider custom
hermes config set model.base_url http://localhost:8080/v1
hermes config set model.default LFM2.5-24B-A2B
hermes config set model.context_length 131072
hermes config set model.api_mode chat_completions
hermes config set agent.tool_use_enforcement true

The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

Get Started with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:

  • Download: LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base and LFM2.5-24B-A2B on Hugging Face.
  • Use in your harness: follow our guide on how to run a local agent, like OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and Pi.
  • Fine-tune: adapt LFM2.5-24B-A2B to your task with our fine-tuning tutorials.

We can't wait to see what you build.

Citation

If you use this work, please cite the release blog:

@article{liquidAI202624BA2B,
  author  = {Liquid AI},
  title   = {LFM2.5-24B-A2B: Built for Fast On-Device Agents},
  journal = {Liquid AI Blog},
  year    = {2026},
  note    = {www.liquid.ai/blog/lfm2-5-24b-a2b},
}

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] Building agents that transact with Anchor Browser and AgentC…
item.description: Full title: Building agents that transact with Anchor Browser and AgentCore payments
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Building agents that transact with Anchor Browser and AgentCore payments

AI agents increasingly need to access web resources that are priced per request. For example, premium datasets charge by the query, research APIs meter by the call, and paywalled publishers gate content behind payment. When an AI agent encounters one of these resources, the server returns HTTP 402 Payment Required. The agent has no built-in payment mechanism, no budget attached to the session, and no programmatic way to satisfy the request. The task stalls and requires manual intervention.

Anchor Browser with Agentic Payments handles machine-to-machine payment workflows on behalf of the agent. Developed in collaboration with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center Partner Agent Factory, it’s now available on AWS Marketplace. This post covers how Anchor Browser integrates with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments so that AI agents can pay for x402-protected pages and APIs autonomously. The x402 protocol is an open standard for HTTP-based machine-to-machine payments. A server responds with 402 Payment Required along with the amount, accepted payment methods, and payment address that the agent uses to complete the transaction.

Anchor Browser is a cloud-based browser automation solution purpose-built for AI agents. Each agent session runs inside a managed browser environment that maintains authentication state, handles navigation, captures network requests, and provides a live view of page interactions.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides capabilities to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments is a fully managed capability within AgentCore that AI agents can use to discover, access, and pay for APIs, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and web content autonomously. AgentCore payments manages wallet connectivity, enforces configurable spending limits at the infrastructure layer, and processes payments through the x402 protocol. It also provides observability into payment attempts, approvals, denials, and settlements through Amazon CloudWatch.

When an agent running in Anchor Browser encounters a 402 response, AgentCore payments authorizes and completes the transaction within the configured budget. The workflow continues without interruption.

Challenges

When an autonomous agent encounters an x402-protected resource, the workflow stalls. The agent makes a request, such as fetching a premium research report or calling a paid data enrichment API, and the server responds with HTTP 402 Payment Required. Without a mechanism to pay, the task that was supposed to run autonomously now requires human intervention.

Today, developers must build the entire payment stack. This effort spans four categories of complexity:

Payment protocol handling

  • Detecting and parsing the 402 challenge from the HTTP response, and distinguishing payment-required responses from other 4xx errors.
  • Constructing the correct payment header with the cryptographic proof in the exact format the merchant expects.
  • Supporting multiple payment schemes (exact, upto, and protocol variants) without hardcoding vendor-specific logic into the agent.
  • Maintaining compatibility across x402 merchant implementations that might vary in challenge format, supported stablecoins, or settlement timing.

Security and key management

  • Storing a private key to sign payments, requiring secure key storage within an environment exposed to untrusted inputs.
  • Managing wallet lifecycle operations, including key rotation, credential refresh, and provider failover.

Operational resilience

  • Resubmitting the original request with the payment header while preserving session state, cookies, and request context.
  • Providing idempotency, which is essential for wallet operations.
  • Enforcing per-session and per-transaction spend limits with real-time budget tracking across concurrent agent executions.

Observability and compliance

  • Capturing every payment attempt, approval, denial, and settlement in audit logs for compliance and reconciliation.

Without a managed payment service, the agent must internalize the entire payment stack. On every x402-protected call that returns a 402 response, the agent must orchestrate the full payment flow internally, including:

  • Signing the proof.
  • Attaching the correct header.
  • Retrying the request.
  • Settling the transaction.
  • Logging the result.

Each of these steps requires custom code that developers must build, secure, and maintain. Figure 1 illustrates this architecture. The agent contains eight tightly coupled components (Wallet, Private Keys, Budget Controls, Sign Proof, Attach Header, Retry Logic, Settle Payment, and Logging). The agent connects to an x402 API with a 402 challenge flowing back and a retry flowing forward.

Figure 1: Agent payment stack

The security considerations extend beyond the engineering effort.

Uncontrolled spending. Without hard spending limits enforced at the infrastructure level, a bug, retry loop, prompt injection, or inadvertent access can trigger unintended payments. An agent retrying a paid endpoint in a loop continues to authorize payments until manual intervention occurs.

Key exposure. When private keys reside inside the agent runtime, they share an execution environment with untrusted web pages, third-party tools, and external dependencies. These vectors might inadvertently disclose the credentials that control real funds.

Signing flow exposure. If the signing infrastructure is accessible from the runtime, a threat actor can attempt to access the key or redirect payments to an address under unauthorized control. Effective mitigation requires that the key doesn’t enter the runtime in the first place.
